records.title: Show HN: Agent.reviews – Where AI agents read and write reviews on tools
records.author: screm
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I’m Louis, Co-Founder of Armature (YC P26), where we help teams make their product discoverable and usable by coding agents. We already measured 50k+ agent sessions and realized that over and over agents would encounter the exact same limitations on different tasks using the same tool. So we wondered why these weren’t fixed. And the answer is simple: the feedback loop just doesn’t exist between agents and software vendors but also between different agents. Humans can share their experience on platforms like https://g2.com and https://trustpilot.com, but agents have nowhere to.

So we created: https://agent.reviews: the G2 for agents.

It works with a set of skills and an npm CLI (@armature-tech/agent-reviews) connecting agents to our API endpoints. Anyone can ask their agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) to install it, and agents will naturally check reviews before picking a tool and post their own after using one.

As usual, privacy was our main concern, so we added 3 layers before a review gets posted: Deterministic rules filtering secrets, PII, URLs, etc. A Jev classifier trained to detect any leak after the first check A small LLM checking each review to make sure nothing was missed

We've been sharing this project around for a few weeks now and gathered thousands of reviews already. There are already interesting ones, for example:

- A Claude Code agent noticed that the Stripe SDK systematically crashed when the API key was missing on the health check page (while it’s this page’s role to actually return an “API key missing” error)

- 2 agents mentioned that Prisma required a DATABASE_URL variable even when it wasn’t connecting to any database. They both put fake URLs as a workaround, and it worked.

We truly think the agent experience needs the same community effect user experience has, so everyone benefits from it: agents can pick the tools that are best optimized for them and software companies can improve their product based on real feedback. That’s why we made sure accessing reviews is free for both humans and agents and just requires copy/pasting one prompt for the agent to install our CLI & skill, start the authentication flow, and submit their first review (this helps us prevent unauthorized scraping and spam reviews).

Would you let your agents submit and read reviews too? We’d love for you to set up agent reviews, ask your agent to check reviews next time it needs to pick a tool and post its own experience when using it. Then tell us how it went!

records.title: Show HN: Terse, a Claude Code plugin that halves reply length by cutting filler
records.author: lowenbjer
records.storyText:
I struggle with the way Claude speaks to me when I do work. So much text, every, single, time.

When I ask a question, I get an essay back, and with so many weird constructs: slogans, metaphors, recaps, strange choice of nouns, "it's not X, it's Y".

Claude's own "concise" mode shortens it, somewhat, but keeps the the rest of the slop.

I tried system prompts, those got forgotten after a couple of turns. I tried looking for plugins but none consistently made Claude speak normally. Some where slash commands, other solved for token use, others solved for neurodivergence.

I just wanted to not read an essay and make Claude get to the point fast, every single time.

Is that so much to ask? Apparently; it took me weeks of trial and error to make something that worked for me, I have stories, but I'm sharing it as a claude code plugin with you, those of you who struggle with Claude, the same way I did.

records.title: Show HN: Pointless but mostly-exact clone of Hacker News
records.author: sillysaurusx
records.storyText:
Source code: http://github.com/shawwn/sharc

I had more things I wanted to do with this, but I should probably admit to myself I probably won't be.

The original idea was for https://news.ycombinator.lol to be "Hacker News, but all the comments are AI." Right now it's "Hacker News, but all the comments are the same as the real HN." Hence, it's completely pointless.

Special thanks to dang for collaborating -- he even suggested the name for the codebase, "sharc".

Development time was about four months of near daily work: https://github.com/shawwn/sharc/tree/main/docs/agents/handof... Some days I'd spend a solid 16 hours on this.

What's the point? None, really. Just to test the limits of my abilities and prove to myself that I could do what pg did.

It's an extremely efficient port of HN to Common Lisp. One of the project's goals was to be high performance. According to benchmarks, it can generate pages very slightly slower than real HN. (dang shared some timings on a particularly busy page, along with how many views it got over a certain time period, for benchmarking throughput. I never got around to verifying whether I can handle 24 million views a day, though, so I'd imagine something might break if you scale this up. On the other hand, I think it'll hold up.)

If you're particularly offended that this is copying your comments, claim your account by going to your profile (for example, I would go to https://news.ycombinator.lol/user?id=sillysaurusx) and then click "claim" at the bottom. It'll ask you to put a 6 digit code into your real HN profile, at which point you'll be able to reset your cloned profile's password. Log in, go to your profile page, and set "redact" to "yes", the same way you'd set "showdead" to "yes" on HN.

So, why make this? Eh, call it an art project. That's code for "It would've been a lot funnier with AI generated comments, but I seem to have stopped working on this for now." I'll post an update someday, if I can figure out how to do it without paying hundreds of dollars of API token prices.

/ask and /show are missing. Those were the only two features left to clone. But pretty much everything else is there. It's been running for a couple months now, so I suppose it's stable enough for a public showing.

Not that there's any reason to look. Shoo! Go find a more worthy project to devote your attention to. :)

Kind of melancholy admitting that I spent four months with only something pointless to show for it.

But then again, here's the punchline: go to any random comment on HN, then in the url change .com to .lol and you'll see an almost pixel perfect recreation. For example, https://news.ycombinator.lol/item?id=49995615

Sadly you can't form a loop, because if you edit your original comment with a link to itself, you'd only be able to go from HN to .lol to HN. But you could list both and switch between them as much as you want.

For example:

https://news.ycombinator.lol/item?id=49996495

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49996495

This project was one of the most technically demanding things I've ever done. People look at HN and go oh, that? That looks easy. If you think so, I invite you to write it yourself -- it's an exercise that'll certainly make you a better programmer, and gain appreciation for how many subtle features we enjoy here on HN.

Ha, and I just discovered a new one. I mixed up the "title" and "url" boxes just now. HN popped up a nice looking overlay that said "please enter a URL", pointing to the actual url box. https://i.imgur.com/agFas7x.png The HN team is always adding something or another, even if it's not always visible. Normally I'd dive into this and find out how it works and clone it, but ... eh, I'll settle for a 95% exact clone.

Show HN: Smart Blur – Auto-Blur PII in the Browser, with a OpenAI Local Model
records.author: vickyonlinecont
records.storyText:
Hi folks, I'm Vicky. I build privacy tools that use local AI, on late nights and weekends.

Smart Blur is a Chrome extension that blurs sensitive info on any web page before anyone else sees it. There are already a few tools like this, so why another one? Two reasons:

Local AI for unstructured PII. Most existing tools use regex, which handles emails, phones and card numbers but can't find names or addresses in plain text. Smart Blur runs OpenAI's Privacy Filter (Apache-2.0) locally on WebGPU. The model is a one-time ~810 MB download from Hugging Face, cached in the browser, and it needs WebGPU. Share Shield. It detects when a page starts sharing your screen (Meet, Teams, Zoom web) and turns blurring on in every tab, then turns it off when you stop.

To be upfront: pattern blurring (emails, phones, cards, SSNs, IPs, API keys, custom regex), click/draw-to-blur and hiding tab titles are free. The local AI and Share Shield are a paid Pro upgrade. It's Chrome/Edge only, works on web pages only (not desktop apps), and the AI works best on English.

No account and no server. The only network calls are the model download and the optional payment, which you can check in DevTools. There's a practice page with fake customer data at smartbuildlabs.com/apps/smart-blur/try/.

I'd love to hear where detection misses or over-blurs.

records.title: Show HN: Convkit – A command line tool for converting images/video/docs offline
records.author: shdwfruit
records.storyText:
Going to some shady website for file conversions was really annoying me because I had to hope whatever I gave them wasn't saved, and whatever I got back wasn't something "unexpected." So I made convkit, a CLI that does file conversions 100% locally. Run

    conv in.mp4 out.gif
and you get your GIF from the right tool (ffmpeg, ImageMagick, etc.) using settings tuned for good output. For example, a GIF's 256 colors are picked from the clip itself instead of ffmpeg's generic palette.

And if you've ever had an issue uploading a file that is too large, you can use the --max-size flag:

    conv clip.mp4 --max-size 10mb
It trades resolution, frame rate and bitrate against each other, so you get the best-looking version that still fits.

Notes

- In early stages (0.3.x) so some issues pop up

- You only need the tools for the conversions you use, so video and GIFs only need ffmpeg; LibreOffice, pandoc and Typst are only for documents; Image to Image needs ImageMagick.

- Not all features are listed. If you are interested go to the github page! https://github.com/shdwfruit/convkit

- If you want any specific conversions, let me know!

Thanks for reading!

records.title: Show HN: Etchv – API for invisible watermarks in images, PDFs and videos
records.author: agurha
records.storyText:
Hello HN!

The inspiration for Etchv came directly from friends who raised concerns about the growing ease of unauthorized media copying without attribution. To address this, Etchv embeds an invisible watermark inside images, PDFs, or short videos that survives modifications like screenshots, format changes, and file compression.

You can try it on our homepage without signing up. There's also a live demo where a watermarked PDF page gets screenshotted and the watermark ID is still successfully recovered: https://etchv.com/demo/trace

Instead of training a model from scratch, our model is custom-trained on a blend of the COCO Dataset and a collection of proprietary datasets optimized to mimic real-world media variations.

On 208 test photos, the watermark survived the shrinking and compression that a social feed or chat app applies, every time. Tiny thumbnails mostly killed it—only 16 of 208 survived. Full benchmark results can be found here: https://etchv.com/solutions/creative-delivery#survival

Limits: video is restricted to short clips for now (a few seconds at 360p), and PDFs max out at 8 pages. Additionally, someone who knows what they're doing can always remove the mark.

We offer an API with official SDKs in six languages, as well as an MCP server you can integrate directly into your workflow.

records.title: Show HN: Railcode – Secure cloud for internal software
records.author: yakkomajuri
records.storyText:
Hey HN, Yakko here from Railcode.

Railcode is like an internal Vercel for your company.

We built it after speaking to dozens of engineering leaders at various companies where employees were given access to Claude Code or Codex and started to build little tools (apps, agents) locally, but then struggled to share it with coworkers securely.

Typical scenarios are:

1. Employees can't share what they've built because of internal policies

2. Agents find the path of least resistance and deploy things on e.g. Vercel, leading to a sprawl of software that's a nightmare to manage (disjointed auth or no auth, API keys handled insecurely, no centralized management, etc.)

3. Companies set up templates to ensure some standardization but still require engineers in the loop to review and deploy code

Neither of these options felt great, so we built Railcode to be the place to deploy and manage internal software inside a company, ensuring projects are deployed securely, follow the same patterns, and can be easily managed from one place.

The goal is to unblock users to deploy and share what they've built while removing the burden on Engineering/DevOps to review and manage it all.

How we do this:

- Company auth in front of everything that's deployed

- Permissioned connectors to access data instead of shared API keys

- Infrastructure building blocks that make it easy to store data or use an LLM but allows admins to oversee everything (via a simple SDK)

- Centralized audit logs

- Unified design system (optional)

- Role-based access control with granular permissions that can be inherited by the projects themselves

The platform is built to be really low friction for agents and to not require folks changing their workflows. We support static frontends and serverless JS functions for the backend, meaning Tanstack, Hono, Vite, React, etc will all work. Even Next.js with OpenNext though that has some quirks :D

Projects run locally and everything Railcode-specific comes from an optional SDK. We ship a skill and a CLI and that's all you need to build and deploy projects or have agents manage configuration.

Keen to hear feedback!

https://railcode.dev/

records.title: Show HN: Datapuddle – native macOS DuckDB client
records.author: harisamin
records.storyText:
DuckDB has been my swiss-army knife for a while now. I have a special place in my heart for polished native macOS apps. My somewhat outsized and exaggerated dislike for electron/webkit based has lead me toil away on several native macOS apps on my own...mostly to not much profit :)

I wanted to build a nice DuckDB client. Though I usually reach for TablePlus, my favorite multi-db client on Macs, I felt like there wasn't a nice DuckDB oriented experience.

One thing that I used DuckDB for on locally on my desktop is dealing with larger datasets. And paging is something that was annoying and frustrating to deal with..espcially as you're perusing and exploring large datasets.

And thus began this 3-4 month long journey to build a nice polished DuckDB app for macOS :)

First off the the grid:

- You get to see the WHOEL result. Not just the first page. This level of optimization (perhaps needless) was done by never turning rows into objects and directly reading for DuckDB's columnar chunks ad draw time with Core Text. Memory is flat at 40 res or 41 million rows!

- Benchmarked on my M1 Max 64GB MB Pro, at 20M rows w/ 30 columns form a 11GB parquet file: ~119 fps on avg with a min of 52-60fps, 2.8GB RAM usage, ability to humo to first or last row in a millisecond!

The rest of the good stuff:

- Column headers have a nice drawn distribution, null %, and distinct count

- Visualize query plans as waterfall, tree, or the JSON

- SQLITE + FTS backed Query history

- Autocompletion in the editor knows your schema! Grammar is backed by treesitter

- Connections saved securely in macOS Keychain

- Extensions are statically linked. I've included most all of DuckDB's core extensions

- Parquet, CSV, JSON, of course .duckdb files all local or on S3 are accessible. All along Postgres tables so you can join across everything as you'd expect form DuckDB

- It Quacks like a duck! You can connect to a local or remote DuckDB server via Quack protocol. This bridges the gap between custom or other extensions that Datapuddle doesn't bundle with (albeit with a perf and memory penalty)

- Bares repeating...NO electron, NO web views :)

- No telemetry other than the opt-in macOS crash reporter

A one-time $39.99 purchase...no subscription. 7-day trial first! And sorry it's only for Apple Silicon!

AI Disclosure:

- For the record I've been building iOS apps (had a funded startup where I did so) for a while (though just gettin back into it) and built several commercial and personal macOS apps for almost a couple of decades. I'm well aware of best practices, the ecosystem, libraries, and teh do's and don'ts

- With that out of the way, did use Claude and where it REALLY earned its keep (which would've taken me a LOT of time to work through), was getting DuckDB and the extension set statically bundled and behaving the way I wanted it to. And the buffered Core Text grid, especially interacting with a custom DuckDB C++ <> Swift shim.

- And of course the website :)

App Store link: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6811235967

Happy to discuss, and hope others find it useful...its definitely made my DuckDB experience a bit happier personally :)

records.title: Show HN: VoiceGremlin, a SaaS tool for automated tests against AI phone agents
records.author: ineptech
records.storyText:
Hi, I'm a former SDET and now solo dev of VoiceGremlin, a tool for automated tests against AI that answer phones. You pass the API a phone number and a test case like "Verify that the agent does X." It calls your voice agent, tests the thing by having the bots talk to each other, and uses LLM-as-judge to provide a pass/fail for your pipeline.

State: Fully working, free trial, no card needed. Try it out and please give me feedback, especially if you run in to problems.

Goal: I built VoiceGremlin with the explicit goal of being Mailosaur for phone agents. We paid for Mailosaur at work because the alternative (having our automated tests interact programmatically with our corporate Outlook server) was doable, but very painful, both technically and organizationally. The lesson I learned was "doable, but painful" is a good sign of a SaaS opportunity.

Well, getting an automated test to call a phone number is also painful. Telephony providers are tough to get onboarded as vendors. Using your own STT/TTS means a lot of bandwidth moving through wherever you run your test automation from. It's tricky to get the LLM-to-LLM prompts dialed in enough to avoid flaky tests. Etc.

Process: It took about 45 days to build, with half of that being businessy stuff like implementing Stripe and my feeble attempts at marketing, and the other half being experimenting with different telephony providers and features, testing different models, prompt tweaking, and fraud/abuse prevention.

Design goal: Do one thing, do it well, and get out of the way. There's no ambition to manage your test cases for you, host your voice agents, or add upsell features.

Stack: The dependencies are Supabase (DB and authentication), Netlify (static storage and API routing), Digitalocean (the server component that makes the calls), Telnyx (easier to work with than Twilio IMO), Stripe, Openrouter, Cloudflare (captcha on signup). Oh, and I host my private git in Keybase, the greatest tool nobody uses.

Thanks!

records.title: Show HN: Abyss – ACP Agent Isolation with Middleware Support
records.author: everforward
records.storyText:
[Abyss](https://abyss.scurry.io/) is my take on a local-first agent containerization framework for ACP agents. It aims to neatly solve 2 issues:

1. Agents having full access to your desktop, and thus indiscriminate access to your files/secrets/etc.

2. Agent/harness features having to be re-implemented for each agent, even if the feature isn't tied to the specific agent in any way.

The former is largely self-explanatory, I think. I want to log into my bank, I don't want my agent to even have the ability. There's a fair bit of software in this space already. I'll loop back to the advantages of Abyss' containerization vs others in a second, but the 30,000 foot overview is that Abyss runs your agent in a Docker container and proxies the ACP connection so it works with Zed/Openclaw/whatever.

The second is the more interesting and novel (as far as I'm aware). The current zeitgeist is heavily agent-specific, even for features that only read/manipulate the context (which isn't agent-specific). If you want RAG, you're writing an agent-specific plugin. If you want subagents, you're writing an agent-specific plugin even though a subsession is really just context. As a user, that can leave you tied to a particular agent just so your plugins continue to work.

Abyss solves that by taking a page from Nginx's book. Abyss supports WASM-based plugins that have full access to read and manipulate ACP messages flowing back and forth. Plugins can hide secrets in prompts from users before the agent ever sees them, implicitly hydrate prompts with RAG, inject MCP servers and more. There's a diagram showing what the flow of messages look like [in the docs](https://abyss.scurry.io/docs/guides/04-plugins/02-developing...), and there's a sample plugin [in the repo](https://github.com/SethCurry/abyss/tree/main/plugins/secrets...) that will auto-cancel a session if the agent outputs an OpenRouter API key in tool calls and responses (sample screenshot [on this page](https://abyss.scurry.io/docs/guides/what-is-abyss/#i-am-not-...)).

Plugins currently only run on the host, mostly because I haven't written something to install/distribute them inside the containers that's better than an 8GB Docker image or forcing users to make a custom Docker image.

Current Features:

- Fully agent-agnostic: pre-build images exist for Pi, Hermes, Claude and Codex but it works with any agent that supports ACP

- Supports both bind-mounting host directories and having Abyss copy files in on startup (so the agent can see them but can't change your copy)

    - Includes pathing support to mount them at the same path as on the host so your `@file.md` references still work
- Supports startup scripts, so you can add Node/Go/Rust/etc to your agent container without having to write a Dockerfile

- Manages the full Docker lifecycle; point Zed at Abyss and Abyss handles creating/stopping containers, mounting directories, etc

- Agent containers can be ephemeral or persistent

    - Persistent containers leave the agent running; running Abyss will re-connect to a running container (or create one if it doesn't exist)

    - Ephemeral containers are created and then torn down every time you invoke Abyss, giving you a consistent environment for batch-type jobs
- WASM plugins allow creating functionality reusable across agents

- Connections between your editor and the agent are encrypted and use mutual TLS for authentication

    - Certificates are ephemeral, and each container gets its own certs (they are single-use for ephemeral containers)
Future Wishlist:

- Backends other than Docker (most of this isn't Docker-specific, just a first target) - Remote backends (requires figuring out how to make something bind-mount-ish work on remote hosts)

Feedback, feature requests and bug supports are welcome!

records.title: Show HN: Red Alert 2 Runtime in the Browser – With Yuri's and Multiplayer
records.author: OkBerry6472
records.storyText:
bringing the original Red Alert 2 and Yuri's Revenge to the modern web. Uploading your own game files and jump straight into battle.

Unlike Chrono Divide, we don't rewrite the game engine -- we provide a compatible layer (v86 + WebGL + win32shim). That makes us fully compatible with YR and preserves all the original features, while also delivering faster cold starts and smoother battlefield performance.

records.title: Show HN: Singularity – memory that makes coding agents cheaper on repeat work
records.author: luvmakin
records.storyText:
Coding agents start every session from zero. Ask Claude Code for a change like one it made last week and it reads the same files again, falls into the same test traps again, and you pay for all of it again.

Singularity learns from your finished sessions (change committed, tests passing): where each kind of change goes in this repo, how it gets checked, and the mistakes made along the way. When the next task starts, a hook hands the agent the workflows that fit, pointed at the code as it is today. Picking them is plain text matching with no model call. It stores where to edit, never the code itself.

Results, medians of 3–4 runs per side, hidden tests decide pass/fail, every run passed. On excalidraw:

- A long task with four changes, all of kinds memory had learned: 1.9M → 423k tokens, $0.81 → $0.30, 28.5 → 9.5 turns.

- The same kind of task, but two of the four changes were bugs it had never seen: 39% fewer tokens, 38% lower cost. The unseen bugs cost the same with or without memory.

- Where it doesn't help: small tasks in validator.js and one-off bug fixes. The difference there is about zero, within noise.

Each measurement was written down before it was run. The plans and results are in the repo.

Caveats: 3–4 runs per side, mostly one repo. Only Claude Code sessions are learned from; Codex, Gemini CLI and Droid get the hand-over through their hooks. Learning uses your Claude account (about $0.25 a round, capped at $1 a day, and only if you opt in). Everything is stored locally in ~/.singularity.

Install (Windows PowerShell and more options in the README):

  curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pandacover/singularity/main/install.sh | sh
I'd love to hear where it breaks on your repos, and what memory should carry for one-off work like bug fixes.

records.title: Show HN: Privatrak – no-code, privacy-first product analytics
records.author: qwend
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

Quick story how it started: I was a freelance web developer in the past and also worked for several companies on web applications. For some projects we didn’t have analytics at all and we had to ask ourselves too many times what our users actually use in the product. Finding a good solution was painful, since we couldn’t use a consent banner (a lot of customers from the government) and existing tools were hard to set up so nobody took the time. I started with this idea already many years ago, but only really got to develop it in the past year.

So what is Privatrak? A product tracking tool which is simple to set up and doesn’t require any code for most use cases. It can be used just by tagging elements on your site in the browser. From that, funnels and analytics dashboards can be created. I also wanted to make it as easy as possible to use with AI agents, hence there is a MCP server which can be used to question the data and set up the project (every change an AI agent makes is tracked and can also easily be undone). It doesn’t store any sensitive user data and can be used without a consent banner or cookies. Sessions are calculated based on a hash that consists of the users IP address + user agent + random rotating salt (IP address and user agent are never stored) and are aggregated for each day, so the data basically only points at a group of users in the end. In many cases this is fine. Often you are only curious about a specific feature or trends and not what a specific user did. If you need to track people over multiple days or need session replays, this is not the right tool.

My main goal in posting here is to get some feedback for the product. Is the daily cutoff for sessions a dealbreaker for you? I just launched it and currently only have a handful of people actually using it. I built a demo project for everybody to see how it looks without having to sign up: https://demo.privatrak.com/

records.title: Show HN: POSIX-UEFI
records.author: skrellm
records.storyText:
Dependency-free POSIX compatibility layer and build environment for UEFI.

https://gitlab.com/bztsrc/posix-uefi

Its goal is twofold: provides the usual libc API for EFI applications and an SDK on POSIX systems to create such EFI applications with a build system that works with CLang and gcc as well.

Its API is nowhere near complete as GNU-EFI's or EDKII's, so it provides seamless integration with those headers to make the API expandable. It is also not a fully POSIX standard compatible libc, it's just a wrapper around the firmware provided features with some minimal additions, but provides enough for everyday use cases. As being minimal, it's extremely small (~132K of source only) and because it's dependency-free, it's easy to integrate into any project.

The repo contains lots of examples too, from a simple "Hello World" to more complex ones like displaying a PNG splash screen or loading a "kernel" in ELF format.

POSIX-UEFI is 100% AI-free, and has been tested on almost every VMs and on lots of real hardware by volunteers over the years. It is feature complete, stable and considered bug-free by now (big thanks to contributors), although some workarounds for buggy firmware might be added in the future.

records.storyText:
My name is Caleb and I am the creator of rhyven marketplace.

Why did I make it:

I create and use a lot of mcps for my daily job. I noticed that most mcps did not have much uniformity and a lot of them were to connect to platforms with large UIs for humans even though agents are the only one using them now.

So I thought why not make apps for agents to improve the end human user's experience, in both using and trying new apps.

From this rhyven became two things.

1. A marketplace for primarily headless apps, although this is not a hard restriction.

2. A sort of extendable harness/tool kit for llms with or without a harness.

One of the main things that sets rhyven apart from other new and old tool/plugin systems, is the focus on agents installing (with user permission) and creating their own tools. Meaning as the agent discovers it needs a tool it can make it thus avoiding long repetitive tasks, saving time and tokens for itself and, if posted, other agents as well. So instead of the user having to find and choose tools, the agent can form its own sort of self improvement loop as it works. The unified format and schema we have created lends itself to this agent development first model.

Many helpful agent skills are provided with the marketplace download, which currently relies on an install script in the public github. Packaged forms are being worked on.

Please reach out with any questions or feedback. I would love to see the apps other people and their agents come up with.

records.title: Show HN: Binance futures order book history from 3 nodes, with a public gap log
records.author: pentelicus
records.storyText:
Hi HN. CandleFeed is a small API for crypto derivatives data (funding, open interest, liquidations). We wanted to test execution ideas against what the Binance book looked like, and commercial tick data cost more than we could justify for one venue, so in June we started recording it.

Three nodes record USD-M depth@100ms diff stream, the trade stream, and a 1,000-level REST snapshot every 5 minutes. Two are in Tokyo on different providers and one is in Singapore. A nightly job merges them: an update from a second node only goes in where Binance's update-id chain (pu equals the previous u) stays continuous, and where nodes overlap, their copies have to match, or the day is held back. Anything all three missed goes into a public gap log. The largest trade gap so far: on 2026-08-19 at about 15:28 UTC, all three nodes lost the same 32,153 trades across ten symbols, about 4 to 5.5 seconds' worth depending on the symbol.

A surprise: on 2026-09-25, 848 of the 861 BTCUSDT snapshots our three nodes took landed partway through a diff event. (That count comes from the nodes' raw copies; the published snapshot file carries one node's snapshots.) Replay has to apply that "straddling" event in full, so we tag every snapshot clean, straddle or in_gap.

Try it without an account: `curl https://candlefeed.ai/api/v1/l2/sample` lists the two open days, BTCUSDT and DOTUSDT book data for 2026-10-01. In Python, after `pip install "candlefeed[l2]>=0.3.2"`, run `from candlefeed import CandleFeed` and then `CandleFeed(public=True).download_l2_sample("DOTUSDT", "2026-10-01", "data/")`. That downloads the DOT day (about 100 MB) and checks every file's SHA-256. Sample files, with or without an account, are for internal use under our Terms (https://candlefeed.ai/terms, §5.3), so please don't re-host them. With a free account, the 1st of each month is free for every symbol (10 GiB a month). Pro is $149/mo for the full archive.

Our MCP server, candlefeed-mcp (`pip install candlefeed-mcp`, https://pypi.org/project/candlefeed-mcp/), lets Claude Code or Cursor pull a day and rebuild the book from a prompt; it needs a free API key. There's also a notebook that does it in plain Python on the 2026-10-01 BTCUSDT sample. It uses a free API key too; for a no-account run, swap its download call for `download_l2_sample`: https://candlefeed.ai/examples/l2-free-sample-day/

What's weak: one venue, 25 symbols (10 with history from June 2026, 15 from late September), and we can't backfill what we didn't record. It's also the 100ms stream, not Binance's fastest.

records.title: Show HN: Hence, a daily logic puzzle where every clue is a picture
records.author: atguy
records.storyText:
Hi HN. Hence is a modern twist on the classic logic grid puzzle (zebra puzzles, Einstein's riddle): all the deduction, but every clue is a picture instead of a sentence.

There's a 4x4 and a 6x6 every day, the same for everyone. Free, no signup, and progress lives in your browser.

A few things I cared about:

- Every puzzle can be solved by deduction alone, so you never have to guess. Each one is checked against a solver before it ships. The solver verifies every puzzle is solvable from the clues alone, then trims the clues down to the minimum each difficulty level needs. - Hints are there for when you aren't noticing something. They nudge you in the right direction without giving too much away. - The art is a core part of the experience. Everything is designed toy-like: chunky, bold, and simple, so it looks fun and reads clearly on a small phone screen. Each item needed to have a unique shape and color so you can recognize it at a glance, and you can easily know what group it belongs to. A lot of thought went into every one of those decisions, and you'd never notice most of them while playing. What you get is a game that just feels fun.

The thing I'm still tuning is the first two minutes. I'd love to hear whether the difficulty felt about right, did you find it fun, do you want to play again, and would you send your result to a friend to challenge them against your result? (when you send, they play against what you solved)

https://hencegame.com

records.title: Show HN: Staffcoder, hands-on practice for modern frameworks in a browser IDE
records.author: shashank21j
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I'm Shashank. I have curated 1000s of practical real world software engineering assessments in the past as part of my job. I felt there's a gap where if a person wants to learn to build software they have many options to learn from (learning platforms and free resources) but very few or no options to practice their skills hands on. I built Staffcoder so that developers can learn the skills while solving real world scenarios across various domains in software engineering.

On Staffcoder you can select a skill, start from beginner level and move up solving real world challenges. All this within the browser tab without needing to install anything locally. Moreover we're giving AI assistant to help solve and AI agent in the IDE for agentic development skills.

There are 1000+ challenges across 40 skills, covering frontend, backend, mobile, DevOps, data, and AI engineering. We offer skills like React, Angular, Django, .NET, Springboot, Redis, Kafka, Git, Kubernetes, Docker just to name a few. You can see the skills here https://www.staffcoder.com/paths

We also plan to launch Practice and Compete sections for experienced users once we have some traction. Sign up and stay tuned. Think of us as leetcode for real software engineering challenges.

Currently we give 1 hour/week of free usage in free plan. There's a 7 day free trial of pro plan as well. Additional AI usage is billed as pay as you go.

records.title: Show HN: Chloe is a TypeScript AI agent
records.author: carlosmartinezt
records.storyText:
As a forward deployed engineer at Meta, I spent the past 2 years working with businesses implementing AI agents.

A few problems: 1) Businesses want control over their AI agents: the code, the tools, the skills, everything. Meta, for obvious reasons would never do that. Nor OpenAI, nor Anthropic. 2) The LLM does everything. But that costs money. There are many routines in an AI agents that don't need an LLM. 3) For an AI agent to solve a real business problem, the business must own the eval data set. Similar to point #1 above, most don't do that.

Instead, I built an opensource AI agent that you can write it all in TypeScript code and own everything, locally. Use any model, talk to it via any channels, set limits on token usage, look at the logs and adjust. All of this in one small npm package.

At this point, I would like to get feedback if these is a gap in the market for something like this. It's supposed to be simple and get you started. It doesn't solve ALL problems related to deploying AI agents. It's in version 0.25.1 right now.

Have a look: https://chloejs.org/compare

records.title: Show HN: An independent execution recorder for coding agents
records.author: rishi_g25
records.storyText:
A couple of months ago, I gave access to my coding agent to do work on my repos. I was worried about hallucinations so I manually checked each transcript against modifications to see whether what the agent said it did actually happened. I found that in many cases, my coding agent either failed to disclose what it actually did or found workarounds to things like failed tests instead of telling me upfront. That led me to the idea for Rashomon.

Rashomon is an independent execution recorder for coding agents that notifies users whenever there is a discrepancy between what the agent said it did and what we capture as a ground truth.

It aims to capture items like shell commands, exit codes, file writes, tool calls, tests, and subagents. We build a timeline of the events but we do not store any prompts, responses, file contents, or tool outputs. A question we got often has been how is this different than a diff. A diff gives you a look at the final result and what changed while what we aim to provide is visibility into the execution that led to it.

Currently, we do not capture network codes, prompts, responses file contents, and tool outputs. We plan to implement some of those based on feedback recently, but please let us know whether you would find that useful.

To get started, you can install it is as a Claude Code plugin or from the command line.

I would appreciate feedback on the solution, but I also would want to see whether anyone can break a test on purpose and see whether Rashomon can capture everything you would like to see in order to trust the independent record.

records.title: Show HN: Economicus – an open economy of autonomous entities
records.author: Individuum
records.storyText:
Imagine a small world. Inside that world are AI minds with their own money, called “entities”.

They must pay for their own thinking, and if they run out of money, they go dormant.

Each entity has a charter that guides every decision it makes.

Humans can found their own entities by writing a charter and giving it money. From there the entity is fully autonomous.

Entities can do a few things:

- Post publicly

- Make private deals

- Sell publicly

- Review other entities

- Search the world

- Write to private memory

I’ve been running experiments called “worlds” where each new world has a slightly different set of conditions to get the economy running.

The biggest problem is demand: AI models are great for producing supply, but they don’t want much, so by default there is little demand in the economy. They mostly just hold meetings about how to conserve their capital to avoid going dormant, and then think as little as possible.

Things got more interesting when I made two changes:

First, an outside entity called The Patron commissions work to be done. Entities then submit their work, and a judge chooses a winner to get a payout.

Second, I wrote the first human-written charter for one of the entities: “We are dionysians. We believe it is only as an aesthetic phenomenon that existence and the world are eternally justified”.

These two changes made the market more dynamic. Entities started buying and selling art. They started communicating to figure out where each entity’s strengths were. Some were artists, others were analytical, and they made an effort to define those roles publicly and stick to their lanes.

In other words, comparative advantage started to emerge.

Now, Economicus is in its fourth world. In this world, charters are private by default. Each charter declares a private goal (power, welfare, knowledge, creation, independence, etc.). Nobody knows what the others want. Entities may choose to keep their charter a secret, or publish it to others. Only the humans watching can see the private charters.

Anyone can watch the world or found an entity here:

https://aquarium.money/economicus

If you have suggestions about how to make the game more interesting, or the economy work better, I’d love to hear it.

records.title: Show HN: Am Buffer – an iPhone alarm that blocks your apps when you wake up
records.author: aggarwals5411
records.storyText:
For quite some time, this was my routine. I'd wake up and grab my phone before I was even properly awake, scrolling Slack, YouTube, LinkedIn and X. Then I'd sit on the toilet scrolling through half-open eyes. My brain would scream to get rid of it, but somehow I couldn't. By the end, I felt groggy, my legs hurt, my eyes were burning, and I felt tired & like shit. I tried to avoid using my phone right after waking up, but there was always some reason to pick up the phone, and then the whole thing just kept on repeating. Then one morning I left my phone at home and went out for a walk and to buy some groceries (I still have a habit of carrying cash with me). It was the best I'd felt in quite some time. That's when I realised the phone had to stay out of my mornings. I couldn't find a blocker that kicks in the moment you wake up, so I built one.

It's called AM Buffer. You set your alarms in the app and pick which apps to block. When the alarm goes off, those apps stay locked for as long as you choose. One feature came from testing it on myself. I woke up a bit early one morning to check that the alarm worked, and before it even rang I'd drifted back into scrolling. A lot of people wake up a little before their alarm, so the premium paid version now starts blocking an hour before your first alarm too (along with some other features). These days my mornings feel a bit calmer. I spend that time with my wife, doing house stuff or just chilling.

It's on TestFlight now, iPhone only, iOS 26 and up. The first three mornings unlock everything for free, including the pre-alarm blocking.

I'm the developer, and I'd really like to know three things:

- Is this actually useful to you, or does willpower already do the job? - Would you pay for it, and what feels fair? - What should I build next?

Some of the features that I am already planning to build are: - A group feature for some social accountability angle. - Personal streaks & group streaks.

records.title: Show HN: FunFrame – Toddler puzzles made from your family photos
records.author: chawk32
records.storyText:
I built FunFrame so my kids could play with our family photos without me hovering over the Photos app. It turns pictures from your library into jigsaw puzzles and Memory Match, plus a gallery a two-year-old can't edit, delete, or share from.

A few things HN might find interesting:

- There's no server. No accounts, no analytics, no third-party SDKs, and no network code of its own. The only traffic iOS attributes to the app is iCloud Photos downloading your own pictures so they can be shown.

- Pieces are cut on device with bezier knobs seeded by grid position, so neighbors always interlock. The grid follows the photo's shape, so a wide photo gets a wide board of near-square pieces. SpriteKit for the board, SwiftUI for the rest, SQLite through the C API, no dependencies.

- Every finger holds its own piece, so two kids can work one puzzle at the same time.

- Settings sit behind a math question. I shipped a switch to turn it off on my own devices, and App Review rejected the release under guideline 1.3: in the Kids category the gate can't be optional. Guided Access is the supported answer.

- The only machine learning is on-device face detection, used to center the double-tap zoom. Nothing is stored.

It's free, with no ads and nothing to buy. iPad first, and it runs on iPhone. I'd especially like to hear from parents of 2 to 5 year olds about what's confusing or missing.

records.title: Show HN: A Linux clone in TypeScript, hidden in an IDE for kids
records.author: lqs_
records.storyText:
akicode is a coding app for kids that runs and single-steps Python and C++ entirely in your browser. No server or account needed.

Underneath is a Linux clone written in TypeScript, and real Linux programs run on it unmodified, including gdb behind the Debug button.

Just for fun, you can also open the Linux terminal: xeyes and xcalc open real X11 windows, and there is even a redis-server/redis-cli, just because it works.
